passage:
At five, Samir stopped at the gate of Uday's birthday party and would not go in. He wrapped both arms around Mummy Damini's leg and hid his face in her kurta. When a grown-up said hello, Samir squeezed tighter. Mummy did not pull him off. She stood by the gate with a hand on his head until he peeked out at the balloons. Half an hour later he was sitting on the step with a paper hat.
At nine, Samir woke on the morning of the class play and curled up on his bed. "My tummy hurts," he said. Mummy Damini felt his forehead and let him stay home. Within an hour he was drawing on the floor, cheerful and calm. Two weeks later, the day before an oral test, his tummy hurt again, and this time the ache began the previous evening. Mummy noticed it came before things he dreaded. She sat beside him. "Something scary is coming up, isn't it?" Samir nodded. "If tummy aches keep happening, we'll also check with the doctor," she said, and they talked about what part of the test worried him.

qa.q: What did Samir do when a grown-up said hello at the party gate?
qa.a: He squeezed tighter around Mummy Damini's leg.

qa.q: How does Samir's stomach ache at nine connect to his hiding at the party at five?
qa.a: At five, hiding brought relief from what scared him. At nine, staying home from the class play made the fear drop at once, so the next time the ache started earlier, the night before the oral test, which shows that avoiding can grow.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he curled up on his bed on the morning of the class play?
qa.a: He was scared and worried about the play, and the tummy ache was how that fear showed up.

qa.q: What could Mummy Damini do next to help Samir face the test?
qa.a: She could keep asking what worries him, plan one small step with him, and check with the doctor if the tummy aches keep going.

grounding: A child hides behind a parent at a party and feels relief (3921); at nine a stomach ache and staying home give relief so the fear starts earlier (3286).

passage:
At nine, Lakshmi sat over her Hindi homework for an hour with only two lines written. Mummy Ganga came in. "Why are you so lazy? Your cousin finished in ten minutes." Lakshmi felt her cheeks go hot. The next day at school she told Gargi Ma'am, "I'm just lazy." Gargi Ma'am pulled a chair beside her. "Let's do one line, then another. I'll sit here for the first one." Lakshmi wrote a line, then two more.
By fifteen, the word had settled inside her like a fact. The class project on rivers was due in eight days, and she did not open it. If she tried and the result was poor, everyone would know she was as useless as she feared. Each evening she found something else to do: cleaning her desk, watching short clips. A friend from the next bench asked how it was going. "Fine. Loads of time," Lakshmi said, and changed the subject. On the last night she pasted a few lines together. The finished work was thin, and she sat looking at it, thinking, see, lazy.

qa.q: How many days before the deadline was the rivers project when Lakshmi did not open it?
qa.a: It was due in eight days.

qa.q: How does being called lazy at nine connect to Lakshmi's delay at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine Mummy's remark made Lakshmi believe she was lazy, and she repeated it as a fact about herself. At fifteen she put off the project because a poor result might show she was useless, and the thin work seemed to prove the label.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when she told Gargi Ma'am "I'm just lazy"?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and discouraged, believing the word described who she was.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi at nine, and how might it help her again at fifteen?
qa.a: Gargi Ma'am broke the work into single lines and sat beside her for the first one. A friend or teacher could do the same with the project, one small part at a time.

grounding: A child called lazy comes to believe it (3187), and as a teen delays a project to avoid judgement (4056); the same girl across years.

passage:
In class five, Shalini stumbled over the word "extraordinary" during reading time. The room went still, and she felt her neck grow warm. She dropped her jaw, crossed her eyes and made the silliest face she knew. The class exploded in laughter, and Shalini bowed. Gopika Ma'am smiled. "Well, you've certainly stolen the show." Shalini's fingers were pinching the page edge.
Chinmay, sitting beside her, leaned in. "What does stolen the show mean? Did she say you took something?" Shalini giggled, her shoulders loosening. "No. It means everybody looked at me. She was being funny." Chinmay asked again later, when Gopika Ma'am said the next chapter would be "a piece of cake." He raised his hand. "Ma'am, is there real cake?" The class laughed, but Gopika Ma'am answered warmly. "It means it will be easy. Asking is a good habit." At break, Shalini went back to the passage and read the word alone. She got it right on the second try.

qa.q: Which word did Shalini stumble over in reading time?
qa.a: She stumbled over the word "extraordinary".

qa.q: How do Shalini's silly face and Gopika Ma'am's remark show that words and jokes can carry more than one meaning?
qa.a: Shalini used a joke to hold on to the moment after her stumble, and Gopika Ma'am answered with a playful phrase, "stolen the show", that Chinmay had to ask about. Indirect speech can be funny or kind, so asking what someone means is a good habit.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she pinched the page edge after the class laughed?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and a little anxious, though the joke let her seem in control.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do when he hears a phrase he does not understand?
qa.a: He can ask the speaker what they mean, as he did with "a piece of cake", and then remember the answer.

grounding: A class clown's silly face after a stumble (3891) and a child learning idioms and asking what was meant (2467), in one classroom.

passage:
At ten, Ishita said to her mother, "The chart on the solar system? That'll take ten minutes." She began it at eight on Sunday night, and it took her until midnight. She had pictured the planets going on in a neat row, not the ink that smudged and the missing yellow card.
At twenty, Ishita had a group report on water use due at the end of the month. Sitting with her friend Swati, she reckoned it would be finished in three days if nothing went wrong. She fixed the deadline for herself accordingly and did nothing for a week. Then her laptop stopped charging. The survey questions were not clear, and Lavanya Ma'am replied to her email two days late. Interruptions kept piling up. Ishita's three days turned into ten, and she was up at three in the morning, still checking the last table. "I planned for the day when nothing breaks," she told Swati, rubbing her eyes. Swati passed her a cup of tea and a plain notepad. "Let's list the steps and see how long each really takes," she said.

qa.q: How many days did Ishita think the report would take at the start?
qa.a: She thought it would be finished in three days.

qa.q: How does Ishita's plan for the report at twenty repeat her thinking about the chart at ten?
qa.a: At ten she pictured the planets going in a neat row and forgot smudged ink and missing card. At twenty she reckoned on the day when nothing went wrong, and a broken laptop, unclear questions and late replies turned her three days into ten.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling at three in the morning while checking the last table?
qa.a: She was exhausted and frustrated, realising her plan had not allowed for anything to go wrong.

qa.q: What could Ishita do next time she plans a large report?
qa.a: She can list each step with Swati, note how long each takes, and add room for interruptions like a broken laptop.

grounding: A child's best-case guess that homework takes ten minutes (3650) and a student's best-case estimate that turns three days into ten (7657): the same person over years.

passage:
At five, Jomon skipped into the kitchen to tell Mummy Jaya a joke. "Why did the banana cross the road? Because... because... bananas!" He burst into giggles and made up a word, "wobbledy-bop", and shouted it three times. Mummy laughed, too, though she couldn't have said why it was funny. Jomon loved the sound of a joke, the rise and the rhythm, more than the meaning.
At nine, Jomon stumbled through a paragraph in class and heard a snort from the back. His ears went hot. Then he pulled his most ridiculous face, stuck out his tongue and read the next words in a duck's voice. The class laughed with him. Tanuja Ma'am shook her head, smiling, and let it pass. At break Jomon looked less cheerful than his laughter had suggested. He sat at the edge of the bench, tapping his foot on the ground. Tanuja Ma'am sat beside him and said quietly, "That was funny. Did the reading feel hard?" Jomon shrugged, then nodded.

qa.q: What made-up word did Jomon shout three times at age five?
qa.a: He shouted "wobbledy-bop" three times.

qa.q: How does Jomon's humour at five differ from his humour at nine?
qa.a: At five he loved the sound and rhythm of a joke without understanding it. At nine, he used a silly face and a duck's voice to keep control after stumbling, and his tapping foot showed worry beneath the laughter.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling at break, sitting at the edge of the bench?
qa.a: He felt worried and embarrassed. The laughter covered it in class, but his tapping foot showed he was still bothered.

qa.q: How could Tanuja Ma'am help Jomon with his reading worries?
qa.a: She could keep enjoying his humour while quietly checking in, and offer practice in a private, low-pressure way.

grounding: A preschooler's silly jokes enjoyed for their pattern (2279) grow into a class clown's joke covering embarrassment at nine (3891): one child across years.

passage:
When Vishal was nine, he told Mummy Keerthana, "I'll colour the whole map of India in ten minutes." He started after dinner the night before it was due. Every state needed a different shade, and the crayons kept breaking. By ten he was sobbing over a half-finished Rajasthan. In his head, the job had looked easy and smooth.
At fifteen, Vishal had a science model to build for Vaibhav Sir's class. On Monday he pictured himself cutting, gluing and finishing in one relaxed afternoon, so he decided he could start on Thursday. He did not count the trip to buy materials, or the glue that took a day to dry, or the practice test that ate Wednesday. On Thursday he found the cardboard was too small. By midnight the model leaned to one side. Vishal looked at it and remembered the map of India. "Same thing, isn't it?" he muttered. Mummy Keerthana brought him a glass of milk and said only, "Tomorrow, before school, we'll look at what can still be done."

qa.q: How long did nine-year-old Vishal say colouring the map would take?
qa.a: He said it would take ten minutes.

qa.q: What connects Vishal's map of India and his science model?
qa.a: Both times he pictured everything going smoothly and started late. At nine the crayons broke and each state needed a different shade; at fifteen he had not counted the trip for materials, the glue drying or the practice test.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he looked at the leaning model at midnight?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and a bit ashamed, recognising that he had made the same mistake as with the map.

qa.q: What could Vishal do next time he plans a school model?
qa.a: He can list every step, think of how long the map really took, and start earlier with extra time for delays.

grounding: A child's optimistic ten-minute plan (3650) and a teen's best-case estimate that leads to a late start (5005): the same boy across years.
